game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"The thoughts are free" ... or are they?

Orwell is a pretty neat little game about the potential dangers of openly accessible (or even not so openly accessible) data and the connections and conclusions you can draw from them.

You start out as an investigator for the project "Orwell", a surveillance system meant to protect the people and prevent crimes. 
After a bombing attack you are tasked, together with your supervisor, to find out who was behind the bombings and to prevent further ones.
As you dig deeper through websites and files, desktops and other material, you'll uncover more and more of the story, the motivations of the people responsible for the bombings and uncover some twists and turns throughout your investigations.

The gameplay is pretty simplistic. It's pretty much like surfing through a browser. You can access (predefined) websites and read through articles, blogs and also social media. Throughout the text you find some marked passages, which will help you with your investigation. You can connect these infos with a person and send these infos to Orwell. You can also decide to withhold some informations, letting events turn out differently in the process.

The story and events really sucked me in and were pretty thrilling. Slowly finding out more about the people, their connections to each other, and also be suprised by some twists, made the game very entertaining.

So if you don't mind simplistic gameplay and reading quite a lot and and the topic of data security doesn't turn you down, this is a little gem to keep an eye on.

I'd definitely recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ohh this is really, really well-done. To a large extent, this is what I've always wanted from a mystery game: being able to/having to think and reason for yourself, draw conclusions, then have them reflect in the game - rather than being taken through a sequence of 'revelations' by the game plot. Partially reminds me of old-school RPGs that didn't write down all the relevant information in the quest log for you and/or spell out the revelations and point you in the right direction - you had to put two and two together yourself. I actually took notes playing this game!

Things that made it a good mystery-like experience: Having to make judgement calls based on incomplete information. Occasional moments of adrenaline rush as you make genuinely (as far as I can tell as a player, anyway) time-sensitive calls. Real consequences that you can retroactively attribute to your actions (and adjust your strategy).

Story and gameplay integrate together very neatly. The Datachunk mechanic feels a bit hokey at first, until you realize that the system really does require your human judgement, and research beyond the highlighted datachunks, to work well.

Technically, this game is probably very easy to "complete", but I don't know if I would call any completion "beating" it.  I really felt clever when I figured out (part of) the mystery myself, and that actually affected the outcome.

Could probably write a whole paper on this game and questions like "what is winning/losing in a game?" "what is or is not gameplay?" "who is a villain and who is a hero?"  if one were inclined to write papers about new-media-like subjects.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike] [b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. [b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. [h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion. [h1]Conclusion:[/h1] [b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Lately I've been finding myself bored with many games. I got through the motions without any real investment in what I've been playing... So, I decided to play something different. In comes Orwell. It's unlike any of the games I've toiled mundane hours hacking and slashing away in any random RPGs that I have on rotation. I've been engrossed in it for the past day getting familiar with the intricacies.

This is a different kind of spy game. One that might hit on reality a little closer than I'd like to think. Even more so if I was prone to ideas of the government watching our every move, which is why I'm an active VPN user. But I digress, Orwell is still just a game. A game where you play a data miner looking into the lives of who you might consider dangerous terrorists to a fictitious nation. I should mention there's quite a bit of reading. This isn't your mindless run and shoot game, or hide from the enemies and kill in secret game. It's not even graphically inspiring but the ideas and execution is solid. 

As you're uncovering terrorists and their plots you get deeper into the lives of those you think are involved and have to feed information into the Orwell system to determine their threat level. The game has you scouring through newspapers, blogs, and social media feeds to gain as much information as possible. It would be overwhelming if the interface wasn't so simple to navigate. 

While progression in the game is pretty linear you do have the ability to impact significant events based on what you choose to feed into the system. There is also an abundance of conflicting information that you will have to make judgement calls on what you want to submit. Orwell do a good job highlighting these inconsistencies. The only thing I might have qualms with is there's no "undo" feature. So if you do happen to make a mistake and upload something you'd rather not you don't have a second chance to fix or update your mistakes. The system for all it's abilities has a permanent function. Like most things once it's out there it's there for good. 

In all Orwell is an engaging game where you play big brother and stop terrorists a different way. It's got a solid story and characters and an easy to use interface. It may or may not resemble some truth to life but in the immortal words of Harold Finch "It's not paranoia if they really are out to get you" and in this game you're out to get everyone.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Final Verdict: Buy [/h1]

Game took me 4 hours to complete 1 playthrough, although you can do multiple playthroughs, depending on what information you find and what connections you make. This game is reading intensive, as you will be sifting through web pages, call logs, chat logs, browser histories, etc. There's also quite a bit of filler information, which is to be expected in this kind of job where you are aggregating huge amounts of data and your job is to sift through that information and find the relevant information.

Not every piece of date is true. There are dead ends and outright lies. Your job will be to try to paint an accurate portrait for your agency to do its job correctly. This game does a great job of putting you in the center of the action as you feel as though you are a real investigator. As the story progresses, you become an even bigger part of the action.

This game isn't for everyone. The gameplay mechanic itself can get tedious at varying times. You really don't stray from what you're doing from the start of Chapter 1 all the way to the conclusion in Chapter 5. So if you don't like parsing information, you will be bored. However, the story keeps it all together and gives purpose to your actions. 

[b]Rate 7/10. Really solid game, interesting story, great ending(s), but the gameplay could have used more variety.[/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While playing the game, "investigating" people of interest and gathering every piece of information there ever were about them, i started to think of myself.. Of my data that is thrown all the way around the internet.. What if i'm, someday, become a person of interest?
This game really delivers its message in a powerful way.. You play as an investigator.. Part of a project called "Orwell". This project uses a mass surveillance system to track any person of interest.
As an investigator, your only job is to dig into this mine of data called internet, look for any information regarding this person you deem as relevant.. And just add it to this person's profile. An advisor, someone who's not you, will be the one to judge and conclude based on the very information that were provided by you.. So you kind of have a saying into the final verdict by withholding any related information or misleading the advisors with non-related information WHICH is something that greatly influences the shape of the game.. Your decisions do make a huge difference in this game!

The story is amazing with a lot of twists to it.. You start on a relatively easy-to-figure way.. Every decision at the beginning will only look as either black or white.. But a grey area starts to form in later stages.. Much more difficult decisions will be forced against you to make.. And that were your journey will take a great shift... But all in all, the story is truly amazing and powerful.
The general settings of the game are fairly good as well.. The newspapers, the unique characters, the soundtrack.. Everything contributes to the general atmosphere in a decent way!

I would recommend this game to those who are looking for story-driven games and who would love for a game that seriously takes their decisions into account.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What would you do if you really wanted to imprison some people that irked you? Obviously, you would scour their Facebook, Twitter, and eHarmony profiles to gather evidence of corroboration between them and terrorist activist cells. Atleast that’s how Osmotic Studios would do it. Although it may be a bit of a crude hyperbole, that is essentially what you will be doing in Orwell, the fascinating game where you play as Big Brother in an effort to keep The Nation safe and discover the culprits behind the recent bombing events in the capital city.

[h1]Privacy vs Security[/h1]

Other than being the author of 1984, the story where this game gets many of its motifs from, Orwell is rebirthed as a new governmental security program created to maintain order and reduce crime in a totalitarian country called, The Nation. Being an all-encompassing program with no bounds in breaking personal privacy, Orwell has the ability to retrieve: medical records, user submitted online information, bank statements, school records, mobile device data, telephone calls, chat room conversations, and pc device data. Your role in ensuring the safety of The Nation is in the capacity of an investigator, one who has authority to utilize the Orwell mainframe as an unbiased outsider to The Nation. As an investigator, you must sift through all of the information Orwell retrieves to discover and submit “relevant” datachunks to your immediate supervisor. What you deem relevant will shape the futures of the suspects under investigation, so take great care in deciding what to submit to Orwell.

Gameplay-wise, Orwell’s UI behaves much like an internet browser with three major utilities: the Reader, Listener, and Insider. These utilities allow you to pull up internet-related articles, tap into phone calls or chat conversations, or remote control mobile/PC devices respectively. Throughout the countless scripts of text provided by the articles or conversations, datachunks are automatically highlighted, and notifications beside specific entries where datachunks are present help guide the player towards progression. Some datachunks will be relatively useless, such as a person’s favorite color, but others will be extremely relevant to the case. Chunk by chunk, you will eventually develop fully-fleshed profiles to aid you in determining who the next person of interest is until the final culprit is found.

[h1]License to Know[/h1]

Using Orwell's features is the crux of the game, letting you slowly form your own opinion on who may be innocent or an accomplice, all while unraveling deeper motivations about the suspects and influential figures around you and Orwell. When you think you've cleanly profiled someone, post-incident reports will reveal multiple perspectives with conflicting beliefs that you may have never even thought of. As each episode focuses on a different character, everyone feels really well developed and sharply defined by disparate personalities and lifestyles. In addition, the more you learn about one thing, the less confident you will feel about another. 

Although the detective aspect of the game begins off strong, it unfortunately slowly undermines itself due to the fact that every clue is essentially hand-fed to the player. Since notifications of datachunks are provided, what ended up seeming to be a neat and helpful feature to ensure that I can progress without too much trouble began to feel like a massive crutch. This created an extremely casual playstyle where I was really just along for the ride. Don't get me wrong, it is still one great journey, but the immersiveness could have been kicked up a notch by providing players a serious investigative challenge. For example, if all notifications and highlighted entries were removed, it would definitely force me to care much more about the seemingly mundane or extraneous text for fear of relevancy. Finding the clues could be as "simple" as manually highlighting useful data. The supervisor continued to nag me about looking for X, finding X, learning more about X, but eventually the clues led me there without trying anyways. I felt like I might as well just speed-read anything without highlighted text in it to quickly move on. 

In addition, certain clues must be fed to Orwell to proceed, even if I wanted to exclude it. The game seems to make a big deal about being careful what to upload to the mainframe, so why force me to make choices like that. Maybe I'm inclined to believe X is innocent, but to proceed, I must upload information that X has a military background in order to create clearance for investigation. Having this feature further supports the casual mindset of submitting anything that is highlighted and diminishes the need to read everything or even care. Don’t get me wrong, the game still provides the players with a fair amount of control, since the endings are vastly different and minor paths will affect the outcome of certain suspects, but I definitely did not welcome the need to have milestone/checkpoint datachunks for progression.

The datachunk system still has some pretty neat features though, most notably in regards to data conflicts. At these moments, two conflicting statements are uncovered and only one can be submitted. You will essentially provide info that you want your supervisor to act upon. Ex. "I heard X was home last night....[phone conversation]" vs "Me and X had a blast at the concert last night [social networking site]." What you choose will relatively dictate what will happen to X. These conflicts returned a little bit of control taken away with the abovementioned checkpoint chunks.

[h1]Complete Walkthrough Playlist[/h1]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6Q75R9yWtU&list=PLeavCsRFiP55ATTks7hLjJY84dnSIXY3y&index=1

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

At first, Orwell seemed to have been just a more interactive visual novel or point & click game, but certain scripted scenes suddenly thrust me into Orwell's world, making me experience the exact same feelings a tech-savvy security investigator would be facing. Times where I would suddenly lose access to Orwell's mainframe, experience a cyber-attack, discover life-threatening secrets or aid Orwell during an active escape attempt. I found myself making motions and exasperations my virtual counterpart would most likely make, and the intense emotions I felt during these moments are something that would be highly difficult to forget as I walk away from the game. I can't recall any visual novels or point & clicks that have made me feel so involved in its world, seemingly shaping the final conclusion to the story.

Even though I have some gripes with Orwell’s progression and datachunk systems, the game is a far cry from being a failure at its attempt to tell a captivating story with novel methods. It isn’t easy for a game to present information in such a way to draw strong opinions from the players, yet manage to continually make their beliefs sway back and forth. The developers, however, knew how to create false trails, dead ends, probable causes and multiple motivations yet skew them towards a believable conclusion. Furthermore, scripted moments that nearly broke the fourth wall created a unique sense of immersion and relatability. This makes it very easy for me to recommend Orwell to any fan of story-centric narratives or spy games. If you’re still on the fence about this game, try the demo. It is free and contains the entire first episode - and it only gets better from there.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intro:

 Eric Arthur Blair (famously known under the pen name of George Orwell) was a essayist (someone who writes essays for a living), novelist, critic and journalist.  He lived between 25th of June 1903 to 21th of January 1950 and was most famous for two books.  Namely Animal Farm (17 August 1945) and 1984 (8 June 1949).  Animal Farm is considered to be a classic of allegorical story-telling and political satire. 1984 on the other hand is a book where endless parallels can be drawn to in real life. 

Where the grim (sometimes terrifying) warnings of totalitarianism, twisting of words, meaning and history appear to become more of an reality.  1984 is considered to be one of the best books ever written (an opinion that I share myself).  Its influence on narrative art, politics and language cannot be understated.  Today’s game: Orwell owes a lot to 1984, right down to naming itself after Blair’s pen surname.  

Story:

One of the game’s themes and commentary is how people present themselves online and “offline”.  This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other.  Cassandra Watergate (get it?!) is on one hand,  an emotionally unstable, childish woman who  does not care about adult responsibility.  However on the other hand she is apparently a activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police. 

Which character is the real thing? That is what helps make the story compelling, Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are.  People are very different online and in the presence of other people (could this man be impersonating another man who might not even be alive?!).  Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to compel the player to continue playing. 

Gameplay:

Gameplay is rather easy and straightforward.  You use Orwell to find data on various persons supposedly involved in terrorist activities. In order to uncover who was responsible and who was not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue.  At worst you have to decide which information is relevant to which character.  You would also have to decide what information is important or valid (someone saying that they are from wonderland is not valid for obvious reasons).  However there is not much of a failure (at least for me )  as all I got was a scolding from Symes.  However I did find myself debating on the various behaviour patterns and deciding which behaviour fits with the character’s overall personality. Orwell might be easy but that does not mean it is not compelling.  Simple but straightforward and very polished. 

Conclusion:

Orwell’s relevance is undeniable, the balance between private and public with the invention of Social media has become.  The encroachment of government surveillance for safety from a threat that might not exist is a legitimate possibility.  The erasure of privacy encouraged by the likes of Facebook and Twitter. Where everything you say and do is recorded to be sold to the highest bidder.  Orwell’s importance as a game will always be relevant while Britain and China’s surveillance states continue to become more of a reality.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Finished in 3 hours, did not replay to look for alternate choices.

You play as a character who works for the government and has complete access to internet, phone calls, text messages, etc. Your job is to investigate people, collect evidence, and solve (and prevent) terrorist crimes. You're the man behind the camera in the all-seeing surveillance state. 

The way the surveillance system is set up is that you collect the information and pass it to an analyst. The analyst looks at the information and decides whether it is sufficient to arrest somebody, or enough to indicate another person is a person of interest that you're allowed to investigate. Over time the network of people you're investigating grows, and it's harder to keep track of their history and relationionships.

If you collect the correct information, you might be able to prevent terrorist attacks. It is possible to get enough evidence to arrest people who aren't actually dangerous or ringleaders.

Sometimes, you see conflicting information (such as when one person is lying) and you need to make a decision. You can't submit both pieces of evidence, you can't delete evidence once you've submitted it (silly, but a game mechanic to make your choices more meaningful), and sometimes it's not clear which one is correct. You sometimes can dig around and find out which piece is correct, but sometimes you need to go with your gut and what you think the people's motivations are. 

Other times, it's not clear that you're making a choice. You can always choose to submit or not submit information, and it could lead to different results. The only way to know this is to replay the game and deliberately not choose things that led to bad outcomes. At first I was just grabbing and submitting all the information I saw, but you're intended to put a bit more thought into it. Is this relevent information? Do you want the analyist making a decision based on this information? Is this quote being taken out of context? Are you encouraging your analyist to arrest a harmless person?

My only complaint about the game is [spoiler] there is only one case/group you get to investigate, and that investigation turns "meta" at the end -- having discovered the ORWELL system you're using to spy on them, they start interacting with you directly. I kind of wanted to see the system working as intended for a few cases before the "finale" case where your subjects figure out what's going on.[/spoiler] I know it's a smaller indie type of game, but a few more cases to establish what you're doing, how significant your choices are, and so on BEFORE it reached that point would have been appreciated.

I did enjoy this game. It involves a lot of reading, and a lot of thinking, in order to enjoy it properly. It's not a good game for people who want to click through the boring stuff to get to the exciting part. In a way, it's more akin to the visual novel genre than it is to more traditional games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that has motivated me to take the time to write a review again, something I have not done in a while.  I'll admit, the title using the name of the author of a favorite book of mine grabbed my attention, and the description of the gameplay was enough to get me to take the plunge during the winter sale.  What followed was several hours spent parsing through the personal data of a group of fictional persons to solve the mystery of a terror attack and to consider the tradeoffs between privacy and security.

Let me start by saying that Orwell is at no point pedantic.  On the very rare occassion a character has been preachy, it was entirley in character for an activist.  This game has you violating privacy in order to achieve a verifiable and practical good; if you are a successful investigator you can literally save lives.  I'd do a diservice to potential players though to say any more than the very vague and cliche question of "At what cost?"

The gameplay is surprisingly interesting and reminded me is a lot of ways of the surprise hit "Papers, Please."  In the not-to-distant future The Party has enacted a new security measure that gathers every scrap of digital information a person could leave.  However, to address internal privacy concerns no one person sees everything and makes decisions.  You play an "Investigator" who has been hired to comb through relevant data as determined by the search algorythims of the Orwell system.  As you read people's emails, chatlogs, and visit their blogs and social media sites you decide what information to pass onto your Advisor.  His role is to determine who merits investigation and draw conclusions from the data you send.  That is to say, the only information the insider in law enforcement is allowed to see is what you deem relevant.  To do your job well you must avoid not only missing relevant data, but oversharing data that could be taken out of context or is irrelevant. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
You've been selected to help the government of The Nation investigate and gather data on an activist group. You're to use their new mass surveillance software called Orwell.  Your job is to sift through all the data available to you, determine what is important, what is truth, and then submit this to the government.  If you do a good job, you could prevent future terrorism.

The gameplay is pretty basic, feels a lot like just browsing the internet and reading things.  You explore websites, chat logs, phone call transcripts, etc and you use the information within to create profiles on your subjects/targets.  The game tackles the opposing viewpoints on mass surveillance, asking questions like - is it ok to spy on citizens for their own safety even if it's at the expense of some civil rights?  And where does this end?

I really liked the characters in this game, they felt very real to me.  Each with their own personalities, motivations, realistic reactions to the events of the world around them.  The dialogue was interesting to read too, though I felt it sometimes moved along a bit too slow.  I enjoyed digging deep in each person's life, trying to determine their guilt or innocence.  I really liked that the game allowed me to impact events.  I could submit data that would lead to a person's arrest.  I could paint the portrait of events to wrongly accuse someone, or I could save lives by taking a terrorist off the streets.

The game has 5 chapters and took me a little over 5 hours to beat.  Once you've beaten it, a recent patch allows you to go back to any previous chapter to replay it and do things differently if you wish and see how things play out.

I do wish the game was longer.  I wish it allowed me to explore more narratives than simply one activist group's possible involvement in terrorism.  But for what it is, I still liked it immensely and fully recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game proves that you dont need fancy graphics for an immersive gaming experience. 

Orwell forces you to rethink the ideas of government, control, surveilance and the right to go : FK YOU; all presented inside the framework of the paranoid dystopian world originally created by George Orwell back in 1948.

Orwell, however is a modern, slick version of Oceania, in which you play a state agent gathering information on citizens in a world that is under perpetual surveilance.  Your role is to select relevant data bites to pass onto a computer system  designed to identify potential threats to the Nation's status quo. 

Where 1984 is a distant dystopia that can likened to far off places like North Korea,  the world of Orwell is far more like the very one we live in. Where the state operatus of Oceania is something that is menacing, power hungry and paranoid, the shades of powerplay in this world is deceptively bright, fresh and friendly, yet equally suspicious and potentially sinister. 

As you gather information you become acutely aware of your own actions and how they potentially affect the lives of the citizens you scrutinize, as you decide which bytes of information will be passed on and which will be hidden.  There are occasions where you will find contradictory information, presenting opposing beliefs, yet easily accepting the vailidy of both in your mind simultaneously.  However, unlike reading Orwell, and having the answers written out for you, here you are  co-conspirator in Big Brother. You start to question the ideas around good and  evil and discover things that potentially, are both.

The concept of the game is as fascinating as the mind games you start playing with yourself as you potentially prosecute or persecute citizens in a world where freedom and control are at constant odds with one another. 

There are more episodes to come,  and the final verdict will not be out for a while, but so far it is a unique and intriguing experience. Possibly the most rewarding asect about the game, is not the game itself, but the things you start to question, even when not playing the game. Though the brilliance of 1984 is in a league all by itself, there is no doubt that this games manages to bring the message in a far more suble way, and succeed in making it relevant to the world we live in today.

That in itself makes for unique and rewarding gameplay, and it would not be outrageous to suggest that Orwell breaks new ground  in the story/novel game genre.

On the flipside, the game is a little too easy, too much handholding and very linear, and the excecution, though good, could have been a lot better. 

HIghly recommended if you are an Orwell fan, even more so if you know little or nothing about 1984.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't know how I came across the game, I had never heard of it until last week. I'm very familiar with George Orwell's 1984 so when I saw this game randomly I thought hell ya.

The gameplay is a bit like the old hacker's game "Uplink". Simple GUI that you, the "user" sit's behind a virtual system to do your work. 

Gameplay: It may seem like you have to do a lot of reading but this "Orwell" system tends to pick out what it thinks is important and relevant information. It's up to you to deem it important. If it is important, it'll unlock new stuff for you to read and so forth. At times you'll get conflicting information, this is the best part of the game as you have to decide, based on the profile you built on the person, which piece of information fits the puzzle.

You can read deeper into emails if you want, it makes you feel more part of the story and the world but you can also skim quite a bit, you'll just miss out on feeling like you know these people, without actually meeting them, it's a little creepy.

Story: It's great. At first I was a little detached from it because I didn't know if a game like this was going to be able to have a deep story. It does. It's told through emails, text messages, phone calls etc.

Took me 6 hours to complete and I don't feel a single one of those minutes was a waste.

The art style was great. I loved the polygon look while still being detailed.

Interface is super easy to use, they did a really good job on this.

The music wasn’t grating as some games tend to be, and the UI was very simple, polished, and intuitive. The filters used on the photos of people to give us our character avatars were a bit odd I will admit. (The fishing picture, bruh Josef, wtf are those teeth man?) It made me chuckle a few times, but it really didn’t take away from the quality of the game. This isn’t a high-impact gaming experience, more-so an enjoyable romp through the hypotheticals of excessive surveillance and its possible consequences.  This was an interesting as well as thought provoking game, and I appreciate all the thought and effort that was clearly put into it. I would surely recommend this to casual gamers. If you’re into shooting zombies on repeat and yelling jokes about sleeping with mothers, this probably isn’t for you. 8/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This was a very enjoyable little game, and pretty fairly priced at just £7. I found it in an article in PC Gamer magazine and decided to give it a go, being a big fan of George Orwell's strong writings myself. This game is surprisingly tense and fast paced at times, while at other times the story can be kind of slow. The thing is, this game shows the player the whole "Big Brother State" issue from the other side, you get to see reports of terrible events you could have stopped and it really hit me very hard.

This is a game that has obviously taken real events into consideration as much as Orwell. The undertones in The Nation and the leadership by The Party feels like it would work well as a prequel to one of Orwell's most famous works, Nineteen Eighty-Four, which was so influential it even got a big screen adaptation and starred a great cast for the time including a very young John Hurt. But I digress. The storyline is based around a crowd-surveilance computer interface called Orwell and is brought about in secret after The Party passes the Secrecy Bill. I won't spoil anything about the investigation, but the Bill is very reminiscent of British PM Theresa May's highly controversial Snooper's Charter.

The fact is, the game has this utopian near-future look while having tense feelings of underlying political risk to every act. The five chapters work pretty well to split them up, and the way the interface works is really nice. Every part of the investigation manages to have a consequence, but it leads to the same kind of point in the end. So, in Conclusion:

Pros:

1) Excellent storyline with strong characters and some really tense chapters, such as Nina's storyark (that was both intense and really threw me off, again one you'll have to see for yourself) and the antics of Initiate.

2) An interface that really makes you feel like the investigator.

3) Attention to detail - the game doesn't hold back with its attempts at realism.

4) A real feeling of influence and a concern that this game may be showing the future.

Cons

1) The lack of potential for follow-on sequels - The game ends on a sort-of final note, as you'll find out if you play it.

2) CCTV or Camera Footage actually plays very little part in the game, with text being very dominant. Would be nice have to access event footage, more access to records in the hands of actual authorities and the like to even out the fact it is a government project, not a bedroom-hacker.

3) The length of the game could be greater, If a longer sequel appeared I would certainly want to buy it!

4) Finally, the route taken is too narrow. This game is meant to show the full potential and range of issues a Big Brother style investigation would have, so more routes for different events would create greater depth and realism, as well as adding replayablity.

So, I thoroughly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys a good who-done-it with a political/ sci-fi twist. 100% a decent little game!

The undertones in The Nation and the leadership by The Party feels like it would work well as a prequel to one of Orwell's most famous works, Nineteen Eighty-Four, which was so influential it even got a big screen adaptation and starred a great cast for the time including a very young John Hurt. But I digress. The storyline is based around a crowd-surveilance computer interface called Orwell and is brought about in secret after The Party passes the Secrecy Bill. I won't spoil anything about the investigation, but the Bill is very reminiscent of British PM Theresa May's highly controversial Snooper's Charter. The fact is, the game has this utopian near-future look while having tense feelings of underlying political risk to every act. The five chapters work pretty well to split them up, and the way the interface works is really nice. Every part of the investigation manages to have a consequence, but it leads to the same kind of point in the end. So, in Conclusion: Pros: 1) Excellent storyline with strong characters and some really tense chapters, such as Nina's storyark (that was both intense and really threw me off, again one you'll have to see for yourself) and the antics of Initiate. 2) An interface that really makes you feel like the investigator. 3) Attention to detail - the game doesn't hold back with its attempts at realism. 4) A real feeling of influence and a concern that this game may be showing the future. Cons 1) The lack of potential for follow-on sequels - The game ends on a sort-of final note, as you'll find out if you play it. 2) CCTV or Camera Footage actually plays very little part in the game, with text being very dominant. Would be nice have to access event footage, more access to records in the hands of actual authorities and the like to even out the fact it is a government project, not a bedroom-hacker. 3) The length of the game could be greater, If a longer sequel appeared I would certainly want to buy it! 4) Finally, the route taken is too narrow. This game is meant to show the full potential and range of issues a Big Brother style investigation would have, so more routes for different events would create greater depth and realism, as well as adding replayablity. So, I thoroughly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys a good who-done-it with a political/ sci-fi twist. 100% a decent little game!

review_text_raw:
So I just finished my second playthrough and I'm highly inclined to replay it again in order to get another ending. I find Orwell to be a fantasticly entertaining game that tested my attention and combination skills. I really liked the case and the parts of the story that turned out slightly different whenever I did or didn't upload certain data chunks. The endings were frustratingly unsatisfying but because of that all the more realistic and refreshing - so far there was no possible way to have an entirely 'good' ending because no matter what there was always something not sitting well with my conscience. I applaud the developers for daring to leave some kind of open ending to the game.

The only thing I found annoying was that whenever I didn't pay enough attention to what data I was uploading and uploaded information that was false or misleading, I couldn't revert the change and I had to replay the entire chapter to get to the same point again. Which sometimes led to me making the same mistake AGAIN because I clicked through all of it too fast without paying attention, so I had to repeat the same thing again. I know the game tells you to stay on your guard in order to avoid uploading bullshit data, but a simple 'delete data' or 'change data' button would have made this a lot easier.

Oh yeah, the topic of government surveillance as portrayed throughout the game was both intriguing and scaring. It makes you wonder how far governments in real life intend to go in order to guarantee for their respective nations' security. No matter what your opinion on this matter is, there's no saying in what the 'correct' procedure is - spying on every citizen and evaluating on that base is no solution, but neither is leaving people to their own devices and letting potential threats go unchecked.

To everyone interested in this topic, I would highly recommend this fantastic game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't normally write reviews, but I think I have to here. If you have any interest in narrative structure, or if you like detective novels, I strongly recommend this game.

The title may be somewhat misleading, as Orwell is not, in fact, set in a horrible dystopian nightmare future brought about by an overavundance of surveillance. In fact, The Nation seems like a pretty decent place to live.

You play an investigator operating the new "Orwell" surveillance system, the most advanced data trawler/compiler ever. It's your job to upload relevant information pertaining to a series of people who may be connected to a terrorist attack. Due to the Orwell Code of Ethics, only investigators are allowed to upload things to Orwell. As a result, based on what you upload, other characters will make some very important, potentially disastrous decisions.

The game plays at quite a sedate pace, allowing you plenty of time to mull over what would be the most accurate and relevant information to allow everyone to make the best decisions they can, which is nice. What's even better is that this really makes it incredibly tense when the game DOES put you on a (usually very short) timer and forces you to make a snap decision that could get people killed.

The narrative has pulled a few dick moves so far (mainly of the "Well that would have been good to know 30 seconds ago" variety), but none of them seem unfair, and they're entirely believable.

As a final big tick in my "things that make a good narrative game" box, the characters all act generally sensibly and behave as you would expect rational human beings in high stress situations to behave.

tl;dr - 10/10 would upload again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

review_text_raw:
https://youtu.be/-dAXOFIVEDw

The Orwell games are simply brilliant. No, seriously, there’s no hidden “but” here. If there ever was a series of games that I can recommend to literally everybody, it would be these two. Not because of their gameplay or their writing, though both of those are still good. No, the reason why I recommend you go out, buy and play these two games is because nothing I’ve seen elsewhere demonstrates the problems of government surveillance better than this.

In the first game, you’re put into the role of an agent tasked with finding the people responsible for a terrorist attack involving the detonation of an explosive at a public plaza. This all takes place in a fictional country called The Nation. The character you play as isn’t a citizen of The Nation though. Its government is outsourcing the surveillance of its people to external contractors who get paid to scour the internet and tap into phone conversations. Your job is to feed information back to a software called Orwell, which stores and processes all this data. You also have an advisor, who only gets to see the data that you feed into the software and they draw their own conclusions based on what information you feed them, which also determine certain future actions in the narrative. You can choose to omit information and sometimes you find conflicting or contradictory information where you have to choose, which of the two you want to pass along, since it doesn’t allow you to just collect both.

You get to violate the privacy of a number of citizens of the Nation and in the process have to figure out who’s behind the attacks. Naturally, everybody has a motive, since the government of the Nation isn’t too well regarded in certain spheres of its population. 

What fascinates me the most here is that both games obviously want to steer you into doing the right thing. And by “the right thing”, I mean to not simply rat out everybody and instead really take in the context of what people are saying. Every data chunk that you can collect in your database tells you what exactly is being extracted from it. So, if, say, a character is angry and says something metaphorically threatening or violent or if someone is generally impulsive, the data chunk reveals that Orwell and your advisor always take stuff like this 100% literally. There’s no room for nuanced interpretation or metaphor. It really makes you consider what information you’re willing to feed into the system and what’s better left where it is.

At first, I thought that this was fairly annoying, especially because it can also happen at times when you really have no other choice than to pick up that data chunk for the story to progress. But that too is part of the message that the game is sending. Government surveillance often lacks context and instead uses isolated details from which to conclude the bigger picture. Multiple times, your advisor draws conclusions and puts actions into motion against characters just as new information about them is coming to light, so the game constantly reminds you that these are supposed to be real people. They may lie to certain characters too and therefore lead you into the wrong direction. And forcing you to ignore that context at certain points even though you’re aware that it exists should tell you as a player something about government surveillance and maybe inform your opinion of it. The game also forces you to focus only on characters that the game lets you investigate. Now this is obviously a limitation of the game in and of itself because the developers can’t create tons of meaningless characters for you to investigate only for the lead to go nowhere. But it also once again comments on how government surveillance can sometimes turn a blind eye to the obvious by merely focusing on whatever is directly in front of it. 

The thing is though that at this point I have to mention that the actual gameplay is fairly simplistic and rudimentary. In essence it’s little more than a visual novel, since most of the time you’re just reading. There’s little in terms of flair going on, you’re literally just staring at a piece of software for most of it, browsing the web or reading along with phone calls and text messages. The second game thankfully features some voice acting for the phone conversations and podcasts, but you’re still mostly just reading stuff. I get that this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea and that many people don’t play games to simply sit there and read something, so the Orwell games won’t be for everybody. But I’d still urge you to try them out simply because of how effectively they convey their message. They’re also not that long, the first game takes around 5 hours to complete. Though there’s plenty of replay value to see how things might turn out otherwise if you made other decisions and maybe played as a blindly loyal character who doesn’t care whose lives he gets to ruin. So yeah, all in all, I definitely recommend the Orwell games.

review_text_raw:
Worth it? Yes. DLC? Yes. Get it on sale? Probably, but it's worth the price if you have disposable income.
I really enjoyed playing Orwell and its DLC. Here's a bullet point of stuff I think is worth knowing before you buy!

-Plot/characters are realistic in a way that would normally be mundane on their own, but this game makes it somehow feel exceptional enough to make the story worth investing in. I think this grounding to reality did a good service by this game's namesake to express the urgency and importance of privacy and compassion, IRL and online.

-Easy to navigate UI, text is usually easy to read. The news articles' text is a bit thin, but if you have a big monitory/screen it probably won't be a problem. And you typically don't need to read every word on each website and email anyway.

-Markers for unread/unused/new "datachunks" that make going back through old info much less tedious.

-Easy to immerse in because you don't have to pretend to be someone you're not to fit yourself into the world of the game. It does feel like a job, but one that has wild stuff happening and your only way to know about it is through the job. Making the player curious is really important for mystery/puzzle/investigative games, and this game did a 7/10 job with that.

-The general concept of this game is so cool to me, I wish there were a lot more games like this.

-This game is much more accessible to people who have little in-depth experience with technology. It does all the technical "hacker" type work for you, and just lets you dig through people's lives unburdened. I don't really care about all the technical stuff involved in hacking & the like, so this was a huge win for me. A game like this can flop because of poorly executed, insanely difficult to comprehend, or super unrealistic hacking mechanics; so Orwell pretty much bypassed that while still making you feel like you're putting the pieces together yourself. (As long as you don't think too hard about it, anyway.)

-It puts you in a position of being the bad guy in a situation that makes you think, "This could literally be happening IRL and I wouldn't know." This game will give you a lot to think about even after you're done playing.
