review_text_raw:
I'll admit, I was skeptical, even with all the glowing reviews on Steam. However, bored with playing the same old games, I decided to give the game a try since it wasn't even 10$. As I started up the game, I asked myself - how this game could possibly keep me interested? It's a game where you're literally staring at a 'computer' screen in-game.. when you're already staring at a computer screen in real life. Not even 10 minutes in and I was hooked. I needed more information and I needed it NOW! I got really invested in the fictional characters stories, lives and background; why did she break up with him? How long were they dating? Why is 'X's relationship with her parents so strained? I looked through every single e-mail and chat message I could find. I listened to countless phone calls and actually cared what was said and listened intently. All the while snickering to myself because the fictional characters didn't know I was listening in on their conversations. 

This game proves that sometimes being innovative and creative pays off. The game was worth every last dollar. It's relatively short (6 hours) and  I played all the episodes straight through, but it still managed to keep me excited and interest throughout the whole game. I kept playing 'just 10 more minutes' to find new information. Although only 6 hours long, I felt like it's the perfect length. Any longer and I probably would have started getting annoyed (because I did want to find out the ending to the story). 

The only issues I had with the game was that it doesn't really explain how the 'upload information' works. It tells you very briefly what your job is - to upload information, but I didn't understand that I could literally choose what information to upload and what to withold. I thought I had to upload certain information to continue with the story - turns out that may not have necessarily been the case. I actually got an ending I didn't intend because even at the end of the game I wasn't really sure what I was supposed to be doing (how did I access information, not upload it but still continue with the story?). You would think 'upload information' would be an easy concept to understand and wouldn't really need a tutorial, but in my case I would have liked a proper 2-3 minute introduction to how Orwell 'works'. The fact that you can choose what you do and do not upload, and depending on that - there will be different concequences. 
The highlighting of relevant text kinda made the game too easy, but I do understand the necessity of the function. Any real-life program such as Orwell would probably have a similar feature that highlights relevant information. I felt like it made the game more realistic because occassionally while reading an on-going chat, I could quickly scan for relevant information that was highlighted - upload it - and then continue reading the conversation. 
I really idn't realize that my actions of uploading certain information would have concequences; I guess I thought the game was a lot more linear, not that I could actually influence what happened by what I did or did not upload. 

This was really unique, both in game-playstyle as well as story telling. I'll be playing it again, that's for sure.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
GENERAL OVERVIEW
Awesome game and "out-of-the-box" genre. Gameplay is very interesting since you analyze the suspects from a digital device, without physically following them. You get to know every small aspects of their lives, but this is a factor that greatly complicates the developer's work. For the ones who love the detective genre, this one is a very good choice. But I can't give a fully positive opinion on this: let's start with the upsides.
PROS
1)Rich and deep story. Keeps the gamer interested.
2)Orwell system is very well structured, its display is simple and not effort-requiring.
3)Plot-twists excluded, the game is actually chill. It keeps you concentrated, but not nervous or stressed. The fact that you can sit down and think of your next move, gives the game the right pace.
CONS
1)Low graphic and audio impact. Although the story keeps the gamer focused, that is probably the only one factor. I dare to say the game has a poor multimedial content. Characters don't "say" a single word for all the story.. You just hear music and other minor sound effects.
2)Too often it remains unclear where "the game finishes and the gamer starts". Has it ever happened to you that you can't understand how heavy will your decision be on your remaining gameplay? It happens too many times in Orwell. It's not clear when your action will bring to irreversible consequences, and this is annoying. Sometimes it feels like the game is playing you, and this is boring because the plot does not prompt the player to take important actions.
3)Insufficiently exhaustive tutorial. Although Orwell is pretty much a game with a "simple dynamic", basically gathering relevant information, I think that the small tutorial in the beginning does not clarify enough what the Orwell system is about. Even though in the tutorial-phase of the game is explained how you should deal with Orwell, the gamer fully grasps the concept after some time, and this is not acceptable in a game where choices matter (especially in one where it's not clear where choices are supposed to be made!). I came from hundreds of detective-genre games but this one is different, the developer knows, so maybe they should have stressed the basic principle more.
4)Lack of languages. This is a text-adventure. There should be plenty of available languages! I understand that this would be an incredibly long job... But this is a noticeable downside. This is quite a problem for non-natives english speakers, and a barrier for non english speakers.
5) You gather information on this system called Orwell, but as you go on with the game, you may find out more precise details, or that the information you considered relevant are just circumstancial. This is a normal day in the life of an investigator. So, why can't the player modify the datachunks relating to characters' pages? this is a forcing. A super complex system like Orwell doesn't allow the investigator to cancel what he wrote?
OVERALL OPINION
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a very nice game, that will be appreciated by most of the detective-games community. It's passionating, you would never desire it to end, it makes you feel a real investigator. Nevertheless, it has noteworthy downsides and there's a wide improvement margin under some aspects. Recommended.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Bottom line up front: Orwell comes highly recommended as a visual novel relevant in our connected, surveillance-state times. Orwell is not a particularly difficult game. You merely act as the conscience for the eponymous automated evidence-gathering machine that potentially has access to everything in The Nation's network. You tell it what's relevant; it tells that to investigators responsible for actually acting as the long arm of the law. Of course, it's still basically in prototype so it's not necessarily that great at parsing relevant information. Drag and drop the relevant information. Think of it as a mystery simulator where you're a few steps removed from the evidence, and to piece things together you have to gather quite a lot of information from quite a few sources... say, from the desktop computer of someone who may only be tangentially related to the case at hand, or phone conversations between people of interest and total strangers. I say "total strangers" but, hey, they were talking to a person of interest, so doesn't that make them people of interest too? Let's get them introduced to Orwell, shall we? In the modern world where conspiracy theories like ECHELON and PRISM have turned out to be very real things made lawful through either everyday foreign spying or antiterrorism bills that authorize domestic surveillance, Orwell is a game about the flaws--and benefits--to such thinking. Are you able to stop terrorism (or, perhaps more accurately, are you willing to make the sacrifices necessary to do so)? Can you keep investigations limited despite your best intentions? Or do you just hoover up everything because there is no such thing as innocence, only degrees of guilt? And... in the end, how can it go so horribly, horribly wrong? Those in favor of a surveillance state will probably be somewhat annoyed with Orwell, but with a title like that they shouldn't be surprised. Those against surveillance states will appreciate it, though they may actually disapprove of the game's level-headed attitude towards such things: yes, it's a conspiracy, but it's a conspiracy of well-meaning people who are honestly(?) trying to make The Nation a better place by doing their jobs. It's a visual novel, so replayability is limited except for completionism and once you get a feel for how the writers like surprises, you can start to see some twists coming--or at least expect twists to happen--but this is a negligible criticism. Orwell is, at its core, about both freedom of thought and the inherent problem with surveillance and preventative enforcement: even with universal surveillance, information is neither perfect nor complete and errors will be made. The game occasionally forces these errors, which can be frustrating, but if you approach it as a choose-your-own-adventure story with a clever user interface these are forgivable.

review_text_raw:
This game honestly fucked me up a bit by the end of it.

At first it kinda comes off as a Death and Taxes kind of game, but no. It is one long single story arch that is honestly wonderfully crafted. My investment and intrigue in the game honestly just grew more and more as the game went on and went in turns I didn't expect. I often found myself expecting one culprit only to move on to another and another and another as I found and submitted more evidence.

I played the whole game in 5 hours, but honestly I will go back for more. I have more achievements to get and I want to see what else I can find. I still have a bunch of questions and I want to find the answers!

Game play wise the choice mechanics here are really interesting. Rather than just swipping information away like you do in most games like this, you are given loads of info and can pick and chose information that you submit based on what the system deems relevant for you to possibly submit. Then there are some bits of info that are game changing. You also can't go back and take back previously submitted information, previous info you have supplied can only be updated.

All the info is presented to you in a way that you can just select the highlighted sentences and submit the info. You can submit evidence without actually reading the whole articles or chats or what ever it is that highlighted sentence is in. However, that is because the system only selects what it finds relevant. Sometimes the context surrounding that sentence can drastically change it's implications. Which is an amazing way of proving one of many points in this game. If you look at the small picture and just submit the evidence based on what the system shows you, you will get a lot more things wrong. I know because at first I didn't read statements completely. Then I realized a few times I messed up, I wished I could take something back but I couldn't and slowly I became more cautious of what I submitted. This also applied to times that I submitted fishy or questionable evidence only to realize a few web pages or convos later that the info was inaccurate.

If you like thought provoking story lines. The kind of game that afterwards you question of you did the right things, this is a great game for you. It's slightly slow pacing at first, but if you can get passed that the game will have you hooked. Another good comparison would be that if you are into Black Mirrors on Netflix, this is a game you are sure to enjoy.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a great gem of a game which involves you taking on the role of an 'investigator', hired to snoop on people and submit information you deem important to the security of the ficitonal country known as 'The Nation'. You are given tasks via a handler who is part of the Orwell system and progresses the story as you pass on details. It's not heavy on politics as such but rather is a 'real time' system and more about understanding people.

Its visual style combines blocky/colourful art with the smoothness of an OS which only has one use. You follow leads and drag info onto appropriate files and whatever you choose to submit will further the story. 

This first run took me 4.6 hours but I think there's more to it than how I played. I chose the hard working straight laced investigator who didn't care about personal issues and basically had no qualms putting innocent people behind bars. I get the impression you can play it differently but perhaps only to a certain extent.

I have to get the cons out of the way: 

- In game the 'relationship viewer' (a part of your display) is rather clunky and you can only clumsily navigate it as your list of suspects grow. I think being able to control movement via arrows oer WASD instead of the mouse would help here. Heck even zooming out!

-Conversations appear to lag and so you can see a reply before the previous message is loaded.

- Finding a 'hot tip' or key piece of information prompts your handler to talk to you (text only, there is no audio, which is a shame) and grey out the text you're reading, forcing you to skip or skim their advice. You very often snoop on phone calls or chat conversations and so this is annoying. Thankfully time is not important in this game but it's still immersion breaking.

What I enjoyed was detaching yourself and being something close to a spy but in reality, you're breaking down the walls of cyber security and seeing how easy it is to investigate something for more or less no reason at all. It questions your conscience constantly and that kind of information can be interesting to process.

I really enjoyed this game, despite being so short, for it's immersive role playing aspects and the questions it raises about our technological future. It so wonderfully sucks you in and weaves a story with characters the are finely tuned. So much intrigue and many times you will consider a decision before acting on it. Thats some damn fine game making.

Lots of reading, so bear that in mind.

Definitely deserves some DLC or a big upgrade including voice work.

review_text_raw:
[h1][url=store.steampowered.com/app/491950/Orwell_Keeping_an_Eye_On_You/]Orwell[/url] presents a decent diminutive mystery with pertinent social commentary through a very unique, novel yet straightforward approach to interactive storytelling.[/h1]

The game first asks you to create an investigator profile through its polished interface, effectively recruiting you in the ranks of Orwell, followed by a stylish low-poly security footage opening that sets the stage for the ongoing investigation. Your role is essentially to play the human element in what would otherwise be an extremely complex data mining algorithm in a surveillance system.

Gameplay in many ways feels like browsing through restrained web pages obtained through a very limited portion of the internet. You select which datachunks to upload to Orwell's server, which in turn unlock more related headlines, websites, restricted documents, private emails, bank accounts, and eventually tap into phone and text conversations between suspects.

New bookmarks just appear by themselves as revealed by your adviser. You don't have any actual research to do, all important clues are automatically highlighted, and as such the game first appears to be completely linear and rather easy. There is initially no clear reason not to upload data other than rare instances with conflictual information, where only one of two bits can be sent.

Then it gets a bit more complex and the story evolves into a satisfyingly more sophisticated mystery with multiple threads to investigate. You can decide to withhold information that you judge inadequate or untrue, and your choices can have pretty severe consequences in some cases. While there are few or no time sensitive actions, tension builds up a lot in the final chapter where you have a limited number of uploads available before a major event triggers.

There is no undo and your decisions clearly define paths that lead to multiple endings. One-way conversations with your adviser also create a pretty unique relationship.

Be prepared for lots and lots of reading. The game features sparse audio and pleasant low-poly aesthetics, but too few rendered footage and no voice overs.

The game's world also feels relatively small scale with only about a dozen significant characters in the story, despite a background of terrorism and international tension. Another odd thing is when you gain access to a suspect's PC or smartphone, only a handful of files are shown. This limited scope nevertheless keeps things manageable.
